title: Building a report
summary: Choose the right visuals, add interactivity, design for the reader, and build the shift fill-rate dashboard as a worked project.

lessons.title: Choosing visuals and designing for the reader
lessons.body:
A report succeeds when its reader gets an answer quickly. Start with the question and who asks it, then pick the visual.

**Match the visual to the question**

| Question | Visual | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| What is the number right now? | Card (or KPI) | One headline value, such as overall fill rate |
| How do categories compare? | Bar or column chart | Sort by value; horizontal bars suit long names |
| How does it change over time? | Line chart | Put the date table's month on the axis |
| Which parts make up a total? | Stacked bar, or a pie/donut for 2 to 4 parts only | Many slices are unreadable |
| Show exact values or detail | Table or matrix | Matrix is the pivot-table equivalent |
| Show a geographic spread | Map | Only if location matters |

Avoid decoration. 3-D charts, many colours and gauges tend to take space and say little.

**Field wells.** Drag fields into the wells of the Visualizations pane. For a bar chart of fill rate by pharmacy: put `Pharmacies[pharmacy_name]` on the Y axis (or Axis) and the `[Fill Rate]` measure in Values. Dimension fields go on axes and in legends; measures go in values.

**Design for the reader**

1. **One page, one story.** Put the most important numbers top left, where eyes land first. Cards across the top, trend in the middle, breakdowns below.
2. **Titles that say something.** "Fill rate fell in March" beats "Fill rate by month". Edit titles in the Format pane.
3. **Consistent colour.** Use one colour for the main measure and a second to highlight exceptions. Do not use colour as the only signal, because some readers cannot distinguish red from green.
4. **Align and space.** Line visuals up to a grid, keep margins even, and leave white space.
5. **Limit the page.** Roughly 5 to 8 visuals. More means the reader hunts for the point.
6. **Label clearly.** Format percentages as percentages, add units such as "minutes", and hide axis titles that repeat the chart title.
7. **Add alt text** to key visuals so screen readers can describe them.

A useful test: show the page to someone for five seconds, then ask what they remember. If it is not the main point, simplify.
keyPoints: Start from the question, then choose: card, bar, line, table or matrix.
Dimension fields go on axes; measures go in values.
Place key numbers top left and give charts titles that state the finding.
Use few colours and do not rely on colour alone.
Aim for roughly 5 to 8 visuals per page.
lessons.interviewAngle: When asked how you would design a dashboard, begin with the audience and the decision they make, not the chart types. This is a strength you can claim honestly: you wrote requirements and documentation for real users, which is the same skill. Say your practice dashboard is a learning project.

exercises.prompt: Which visual best shows how fill rate changed month by month over a year?
exercises.explanation: A line chart with months on the axis shows a trend over time. A pie shows parts of a whole, and a card shows a single value.

exercises.prompt: Which visual is best for showing a single headline number such as the overall fill rate?
exercises.explanation: A card displays one value prominently.

exercises.prompt: A pharmacy staffing manager wants to know where shifts go unfilled. Describe a one-page layout: which visuals, where they go, and one design choice you make to help the reader.
exercises.answer: Top row: cards for overall fill rate, shifts requested and average minutes to fill. Middle left: a line chart of fill rate by month to show the trend. Middle right: a bar chart of fill rate by pharmacy, sorted lowest first, so the weak sites are obvious. Bottom: a bar chart of cancellation reasons. Slicers for date and region. Design choices: titles that state the finding, one highlight colour for pharmacies below target, and no more than about seven visuals.
rubric: A trend visual over time and a comparison visual by pharmacy
Places key numbers prominently and keeps the page uncluttered
Mentions at least one specific readability choice, such as sorting, titles or colour use

lessons.title: Slicers, filters, drill-through and interactions
lessons.body:
Interactivity is a big part of why people use Power BI instead of a static spreadsheet. A few tools do most of the work.

**Slicers.** A slicer is a visual that filters the page. Add one from the Visualizations pane and drop a field such as `Dates[Month]` or `Pharmacies[region]` on it. It can be a list, dropdown, buttons or a date range slider. Slicers filter through the relationships you built, which is why they should use dimension fields. Keep them together and visible, and use at most three or four.

**The Filters pane.** Filters can be applied at three levels:

| Level | Applies to |
|---|---|
| Visual | one chart only |
| Page | every visual on the page |
| Report | every page |

Use a filter, not a slicer, when the reader should not change it, for example excluding test shifts from the whole report.

**Cross-filtering and highlighting.** By default, clicking a bar filters or highlights the other visuals on the page. Hold Ctrl to select several. Use Format > Edit interactions to stop a visual from affecting another, for example so a trend line is not filtered by a click on its neighbour.

**Drill down.** Put several fields in a chart axis as a hierarchy, such as Year, Month. The drill buttons on the visual let readers move from year to month and back.

**Drill-through.** This lets a reader jump from a summary to detail about one item:

1. Add a new page, called for example "Pharmacy detail".
2. Drag `Pharmacies[pharmacy_name]` into the **Drill-through** well of that page.
3. Build visuals on the page for that single pharmacy: fill rate by month, cancellation reasons, a table of shifts.
4. On the main page, right-click a pharmacy bar and choose Drill through > Pharmacy detail. The detail page opens filtered to that pharmacy, and a back button appears.

**Tooltips and bookmarks.** Hovering shows a tooltip, which you can customise with a small report page. Bookmarks save a view, and with buttons let readers switch between views. Learn these after the basics.

Be careful that too much interaction hides the main message. Set a sensible default view so the report makes sense before anyone clicks. Test by clicking everything: one broken interaction can show wrong numbers without any error message.
keyPoints: Slicers filter the page and work best on dimension fields.
Filters can be set at visual, page or report level.
Edit interactions controls how visuals affect each other.
Drill-through jumps to a detail page filtered to the selected item.
Set a clear default view and click through every interaction before sharing.
lessons.interviewAngle: If asked what makes a dashboard useful, mention a summary page plus drill-through to detail. Explain it as you would to a user: "click a pharmacy to see its own page". Be honest that you have built these in practice and in no production role.

exercises.prompt: A reader sees a low fill rate for Harbor and wants a separate page showing only Harbor's detail. Which feature provides this?
exercises.explanation: Drill-through opens a detail page filtered to the item the reader right-clicked. A page filter would fix the filter for everyone.

exercises.prompt: Which filter level applies to every page of a report: visual, page or report?
exercises.explanation: Report-level filters apply to all pages; page-level to one page; visual-level to one chart.

exercises.prompt: Describe the steps to build a drill-through page so a reader can right-click a pharmacy on the summary page and see that pharmacy's monthly fill rate and cancellation reasons.
exercises.answer: Add a new page and name it Pharmacy detail. Drag Pharmacies[pharmacy_name] into the Drill-through well on that page. Build a line chart of Fill Rate by month and a bar chart of cancellation reasons on the page, using the shared measures. On the summary page, right-click a pharmacy in a visual and choose Drill through > Pharmacy detail. The page opens filtered to that pharmacy, with a back button to return.
rubric: Creates a new page for the detail
Adds the pharmacy field to the Drill-through well
Builds the monthly and cancellation visuals on that page
Explains the right-click action from the summary page

lessons.title: Worked project: the shift fill-rate dashboard
lessons.body:
Here is the whole workflow on the practice data in `assets/content/datasets/`. It stands in for what you reported on in SQL: shift fill rate, time to fill and cancellation reasons. The data is fictional, so it is safe to show.

**1. Get and clean.** Load `shifts.csv` (id, pharmacy_id, pharmacist_id, requested_at, filled_at, starts_at, status, cancel_reason, is_emergency; 1019 rows) and `pharmacies.csv` (id, name, city, state; 40 rows). In Power Query: set the three datetime columns to Date/Time, rename `id` to `shift_id` and `name` to `pharmacy_name`, and add:

- `request_date`: Date Only from `requested_at`.
- `hours_to_fill`: `filled_at` minus `requested_at`, converted to hours (null when `filled_at` is empty).
- `is_filled`: 1 when `filled_at` has a value, otherwise 0 (Add Column > Conditional Column).

**2. Model.** Create the `Dates` table and mark it. Relate `Pharmacies[id]` to `Shifts[pharmacy_id]` and `Dates[Date]` to `Shifts[request_date]`, both one-to-many, single direction.

**3. Measures.**

```text
Total Shifts = COUNTROWS(Shifts)
Filled Shifts = CALCULATE([Total Shifts], Shifts[is_filled] = 1)
Cancelled Shifts = CALCULATE([Total Shifts], Shifts[status] = "cancelled")
Fill Rate = DIVIDE([Filled Shifts], [Total Shifts])
Cancel Rate = DIVIDE([Cancelled Shifts], [Total Shifts])
Avg Hours to Fill = AVERAGE(Shifts[hours_to_fill])
```

Format the two rates as percentages and `Avg Hours to Fill` with two decimals.

**4. Check.** Before drawing anything, put the measures in a card or table and compare with a SQL query on the same file. On the whole dataset you should see Total Shifts 1019, Filled Shifts 906 (Fill Rate 88.9%), Cancelled Shifts 171 (Cancel Rate 16.8%) and Avg Hours to Fill 9.52. Combined rates come from totals: if January has 20 requests with 18 filled and February has 30 with 21 filled, the two months together are 39 / 50 = 78.0%, not the average of 90% and 70%.

**5. Layout.**

| Area | Visual |
|---|---|
| Top row | Cards: Fill Rate, Total Shifts, Cancel Rate, Avg Hours to Fill |
| Middle left | Line chart: Fill Rate by `Dates[Month]` |
| Middle right | Bar chart: Fill Rate by `Pharmacies[state]`, sorted ascending |
| Bottom | Bar chart: Cancelled Shifts by `cancel_reason` |
| Left side | Slicers: month, state |

Add a drill-through page for one pharmacy. Give each visual a title that states what it shows, and keep one highlight colour for results below target.

**6. Publish** (next unit) and write a short note: data source, date range, definitions ("fill rate = shifts with a filled time / all requested shifts") and known gaps. Definitions are as valuable as charts, because stakeholders argue about what a metric means.
keyPoints: Build in order: clean, model, measure, check, then visuals.
Define Total Shifts, Filled Shifts, Fill Rate, Cancel Rate and Avg Hours to Fill as measures.
Verify measures against a SQL query before building charts: 1019 shifts, 906 filled, 88.9%.
Combined rates are computed from totals (39/50), not by averaging months.
Use sample data, document metric definitions and keep the page uncluttered.
lessons.interviewAngle: This project is your proof of learning. Describe it plainly: "a practice dashboard built on sample shift data that mirrors the reporting I did in SQL". Walk through the measures and the check against SQL. Do not imply it came from the employer's real data or that you used Power BI at work.

exercises.prompt: Which is the correct definition of the Fill Rate measure in the project?
exercises.explanation: The fill rate is filled shifts as a share of all shifts, and DIVIDE handles a zero denominator safely.

exercises.prompt: January has 20 requested shifts with 18 filled, and February has 30 requested with 21 filled. What is the fill rate across both months combined, as a percentage?
exercises.explanation: 39 filled divided by 50 requested is 0.78. Averaging 90% and 70% would wrongly give 80%.

exercises.prompt: Walk through, in order, how you would build the shift fill-rate dashboard from two CSV files and make sure the numbers are correct.
exercises.answer: Load shifts and pharmacies in Power Query, set types, add a date-only request date, hours to fill and an is_filled flag. Build a Dates table, mark it, and create one-to-many relationships from Pharmacies and Dates to Shifts. Write measures: Total Shifts, Filled Shifts, Cancelled Shifts, Fill Rate, Cancel Rate and Avg Hours to Fill. Put the measures in a card or table and compare with a SQL query on the same data (1019 shifts, 906 filled, 88.9%). Then build cards, a monthly line chart, a bar chart by state, a cancellation reasons chart and slicers, add a drill-through page, and document the metric definitions.
rubric: Cleans and shapes data in Power Query first
Builds the date table and relationships
Defines measures including Fill Rate with DIVIDE
Checks measures against SQL or a manual count
Builds sensible visuals and documents definitions
